newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Daiei seen struggling to stay profitable.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Daiei seen struggling to stay profitable.

text.p: Japan's largest retail chain operator is expected to stay in the black when it announces its annual business results later this week, but only because it sold off some of its assets, analysts say.
They also said sluggish sales and an image problem meant Daiei Inc would struggle to make a profit for the current business year which began on March 1.
"The company will likely be in the red in 1997/98 as it continues to struggle to rebuild its retail operations," said Masahiro Matsuoka, an analyst at BZW Securities (Japan) Ltd.
Daiei, which operates stores from Hokkaido to Okinawa, is scheduled to announce its results on Friday.
Last month Daiei revised down its earnings forecast for the 1996/97 business year.

The company said that it expects parent sales of 2.51 trillion yen ($19.9 billion), down from the previous forecast of 2.52 trillion yen ($20 billion), and parent current profit of 500 million yen ($3.96 million), down from 13 billion yen ($103 million). Daiei posted parent sales of 2.50 trillion yen ($19.8 billion) and a parent current profit of 25.04 billion yen ($198 million) in 1995/96.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses made on investments and other non-operating activities.

Daiei said sales in the first half of the business year were hit by a food poisoning epidemic, which triggered health fears about certain fresh food products, and by a unusually cool summer, depressing sales of clothing and outdoor goods.
It added that winter apparel sales were also sluggish.

The analysts said the retailer would have fallen into the red in the last business year if it had not sold 14 billion yen ($111 million) worth of shares it held in major Japanese department store Takashimaya Co Ltd to another Japanese department store, Printemps Ginza SA, in August.
Analysts said the sluggish sales were also a result of an image problem arising out of staff cuts and Daiei's emphasis on self-service shopping in the last several years.
The retailer fell out of favour with some Japanese consumers who pefer face-to-face service and who began to doubt the quality of Daiei's products and services, the analysts said.
Daiei president Isao Nakauchi admitted last year that the restructuring had gone too far and said the company would put more staff into its stores.
However, analysts were doubtful whether the policy change would bring any immediate results.
"It will take at least several years for Daiei to rebuild its image," one analyst said.
Ken Egusa, analyst at UBS Securities Ltd, said he expects Daiei to post parent sales of 2.5 trillion yen ($19.8 billion) in 1996/97, but added the actual figure could be lower.
Daiei has also said it would cut its interest-bearing debts by 160 billion yen ($1.26 billion) to 500 billion yen ($3.96 billion) by the end of March 2002. ($1=126 yen)
